# Model-based evaluation of an infant HPV prophylactic vaccination program in Nigeria

Robyn M. Stuart1\*^, Umeh Ifeoma Blessing2, Christopher Gill1, Jamie A. Cohen1  
*1 Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Seattle, USA; 2 Department of Clinical Pharmacy, Nnamdi Azikiwe University, Awka, Nigeria; ^ Contractor on assignment*  
*Corresponding author: Robyn Stuart, info@hpvsim.org*

# 

# Abstract

**Background**: Nigeria introduced single-dose HPV vaccination for girls aged 9–14 in 2023, reaching approximately 60% aggregate coverage by 2025 with a strong education gradient favouring in-school girls. In this study we used a Nigeria-calibrated model of HPV transmission to quantify the residual cervical cancer burden under continued adolescent delivery, assess how additional screening scale-up and equity assumptions modify it, and identify the effective coverage requirements for an infant HPV vaccination programme to be non-inferior to the existing adolescent strategy.

**Methods**: We used HPVsim (v3.1.0), an agent-based microsimulation calibrated to Nigerian sexual behaviour, HPV prevalence, and cervical cancer incidence, to project new cervical cancer cases and age-standardised incidence over 2025–2100 under nine scenarios plus a 3 × 3 infant coverage-by-efficacy sensitivity grid. Scenarios varied vaccination delivery mode (status-quo adolescent, WHO 90-70-90 adolescent scale-up, and 60/75/90% infant delivery), screening coverage (opportunistic 15% vs. scaled 70% aggregate), and the education correlation on both vaccination and screening (odds ratio 1 vs. 5). Each scenario was run at 9 replicates (3 calibration draws × 3 seeds).

**Results**: Continuation of Nigeria's current adolescent programme was projected to avert 1.77 million cervical cancer cases over 2025–2100 (a 53% reduction relative to no vaccination), with age-standardised incidence falling from 19.5 to 7.2 per 100,000 by 2100. However, 86% of the near-term (2025–2075) burden fell on the pre-2015 birth cohort — women already outside the vaccination target age — leaving approximately 969,000 residual cases in this cohort. WHO screening scale-up averted a further 442,000 cases (28%), of which 63% fell in the pre-2015 cohort. Under our baseline assumption of a 5-fold education gradient on screening, correlated delivery generated 6% more cancers in the vaccine-targetable cohorts than equitable delivery at the same aggregate coverage. Infant vaccination at 90% coverage and 95% effective vaccine efficacy at exposure produced outcomes comparable to full WHO adolescent scale-up (51% vs. 56% reduction in vax-targetable cohort cancers), but at Nigeria's DTP3-anchored 62% coverage floor combined with reduced efficacy at exposure (50%) the strategy averted only 20% of these cancers.

**Conclusions**: The near-term cervical cancer burden in Nigeria is dominated by cohorts vaccination cannot reach; scaling screening for them is the more consequential lever over the coming three decades. For the vaccine-targetable cohorts, infant delivery is an attractive route around the education gradient that mediates access to vaccination and screening — but only if effective vaccine efficacy at exposure and delivery coverage together meet the threshold set by Equation 1. Empirical data on infant HPV vaccine durability, immunogenicity, and delivery coverage through the routine childhood series are the missing pieces that would enable a policy decision.

# Introduction

Despite incredibly effective prophylactic vaccines that prevent the acquisition of human papillomavirus (HPV), the causal agent of invasive cervical cancer, global coverage remains low, with only 27% of girls having received the HPV vaccine in 2023 (1). This figure stands in stark contrast to reported levels of vaccination coverage for infants and toddlers, with an estimated 84% of infants having received three doses of the vaccine against diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis (DTP3) in 2023\. One explanation for this significant discrepancy is the age of vaccination, with the HPV vaccine targeted to pre-adolescent girls, an age group that has not been traditionally reached with routine health care services. Many countries have leveraged school-based programs, and while such programs can be successful (2,3), they exclude out-of-school youth who also tend to be at higher risk for early sexual debut, concurrent sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and other conditions that might exacerbate their risk of HPV acquisition and persistence (4). Additionally, targeting girls just prior to sexual debut with a vaccine that prevents acquisition of an STI is potentially stigmatizing, and this has fueled vaccine hesitancy that limits uptake (5). In contrast, childhood vaccination series are a routine and established service that garner high levels of coverage even in the poorest and lowest resource settings.

There have been several studies to date examining the potential benefit of *broadening* the upper age of prophylactic HPV vaccination — that is, catch-up vaccination for older girls and young women who were beyond the recommended age at the time of vaccine introduction — with evidence of decreasing marginal utility at older ages (6,7). The alternative direction, *shifting the age of routine vaccination downwards* into the childhood immunisation series, is conceptually distinct and has received far less attention. For vaccines with limited duration of protection, vaccination should occur as close to exposure as possible, but given evidence that a single dose of HPV vaccine provides durable protection against HPV infection and precancer for up to a decade in adolescent and young-adult recipients (8–12), it is feasible to consider vaccination strategies targeted some years before exposure. Arguments for this proposal include the ability to establish higher coverage levels; reduced delivery costs associated with adding a vaccine to an existing platform; and hope that targeting infants would delink the vaccine from an STI vaccine and associated vaccine hesitancy. Arguments against this approach include the uncertainty regarding the ability to induce durable immune responses that will last until and beyond sexual debut and peak HPV exposure; cost of doses procured for infants on top of those for pre-adolescent girls; and opportunity cost of not establishing and investing in a health care platform to reach pre-adolescent girls with health and social services they might not otherwise access.

Our study focuses on Nigeria, Africa's most populous country with an estimated population exceeding 240 million (\[ref UN WPP\]) and an estimated 12,000 new cases of cervical cancer and almost 8,000 cervical cancer deaths annually (\[ref GLOBOCAN\]). Nigeria introduced HPV vaccination through Gavi support in October 2023 using a single-dose schedule of quadrivalent vaccine (HPV 16/18/6/11), targeting girls aged 9–14 through a phased rollout: an initial 15-state launch in October 2023 followed by expansion to the remaining 21 states plus the Federal Capital Territory in mid-2024 (\[ref NPHCDA\]). Within the first year the programme vaccinated more than 15 million girls, representing approximately 85% coverage of the target age group nationally, although coverage varies substantially between states — from over 95% in some southern states to below 60% in parts of the north-east and north-west where insecurity and lower baseline immunisation coverage complicate delivery (\[ref\]). School-based delivery has been the core modality, with community-based outreach through health facilities, door-to-door campaigns, and partnerships with community leaders reaching girls not currently enrolled in school. Complementary strategies are expensive to implement — the current programme's introduction and rollout costs are estimated at US$18.1 million, with a per-fully-immunised-girl cost of US$3.98 over a 5-year period (14).

Cervical cancer control in Nigeria is further constrained by the near-absence of population-based secondary prevention: Nigeria lacks a tailored national cervical cancer control policy or population-based screening programme, and coverage of the opportunistic screening that does exist reaches only about 10% of women in their lifetime (\[ref PMC9116993\]). This means that the burden of disease over the next several decades depends predominantly on what can be achieved by primary prevention through vaccination. The next critical stages for Nigeria are therefore: (i) maintaining or scaling the vaccination coverage achieved during the initial 9–14 rollout, especially among out-of-school girls who are otherwise excluded from school-based delivery; and (ii) considering alternative delivery strategies that could reach a broader fraction of the birth cohort. It is worth investigating what level of efficacy would be required for an infant HPV vaccine to be competitive with the existing strategy of vaccinating 9–14 year olds — a strategy that has demonstrated high efficacy but faces difficulties in sustaining high coverage, especially among girls at greatest risk.

To explore the utility of HPV vaccinations in younger children, in this study we focused on the two key parameters: (1) uptake of the vaccine by age group (the key advantage to the infant/toddler strategy); and (2) efficacy of the vaccine over time (the potential limitation of this strategy). Our analysis estimated total cases of cervical cancer and deaths averted across a range of scenarios.

# Methods

## Model overview and Nigeria calibration

We used HPVsim (version 3.1.0), an open-source agent-based microsimulation model of HPV transmission and cervical disease progression described in detail elsewhere (15). HPVsim represents a sexually-networked female and male population aged 0–100, in which HPV is transmitted through partnerships across marital, casual, and one-off layers. Nine HPV genotypes are modelled explicitly: the seven oncogenic types included in the 9-valent vaccine (HPV 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58), plus HPV 6 and 11, which cause anogenital warts but not cancer. HPV infections progress through pre-cancerous (pre-CIN and CIN) states with genotype- and age-specific transition rates, and a small fraction of persistent infections progress to invasive cervical cancer. Nigeria-specific demographic dynamics are captured through built-in age- and sex-stratified fertility and mortality inputs, so that projected population growth to 2100 is reflected in counterfactual denominators.

We calibrated the model to Nigeria using the same iterative Optuna-based procedure previously applied to India (15) and to 30 sub-Saharan African countries (16). Fitting targets were: age-specific new cervical cancer cases, age-standardised cancer incidence (WHO 2000 standard), HPV genotype distribution in cancer and in high-grade lesions, and age-specific HPV DNA prevalence in women aged 15–49. Free parameters governed the transmission probability per act, the cross-layer transmission scalar, cross-immunity between genotypes, and per-genotype natural-history parameters (transformation probability, CIN duration, and progression rate). The best-fitting parameter set achieved a mismatch of 8.2 and reproduced the reported Nigeria ASR of 18.4 per 100,000. Calibration diagnostics — the age-mixing pattern, sexual debut and partnership distributions, and target vs. simulated outputs — are shown in Figures S1 and S2, with the top-N ensemble time series in Figure S3.

## Effective coverage, equivalence, and treatment of waning

Whether infant vaccination compares favourably to adolescent vaccination depends on the *effective coverage* of each programme at the time of HPV exposure — the product of vaccine coverage and vaccine efficacy at exposure. Under stable duration of protection, a shift from adolescent to infant delivery yields equivalent projected cervical cancer burden under the model whenever

VE\_i · VC\_i ≥ VE\_a · VC\_a		 (Equation 1)

where subscripts *a* and *i* denote adolescents and infants respectively, VE denotes vaccine efficacy against acquisition at exposure, and VC denotes coverage of the target cohort. Figure 1A plots the coverage/efficacy isocurves implied by Equation 1 assuming an adolescent-delivery efficacy of 95% and varying adolescent coverage (VCA) between 10% and 90%. Throughout this paper we define the primary health outcome as cumulative new cervical cancer cases 2025–2100, with age-standardised cancer incidence at 2100 as a secondary outcome.

Because infant vaccination is administered in the first months of life while peak HPV exposure in Nigeria follows sexual debut at a median age of 17.9 years (19), with cumulative exposure risk continuing to build through the mid-20s, durability of protection across this ~15–25-year gap is the central biological uncertainty for this delivery strategy. Rather than fit an explicit waning function inside HPVsim, we take advantage of the observation that any biological explanation for a durability shortfall reduces to a single quantity: the effective VE remaining at exposure, the fraction of administered efficacy that persists to the age each cohort acquires HPV. Two qualitatively distinct mechanisms could produce the same shortfall relative to the ~95% adolescent-equivalent benchmark (Figure 1B, C): (a) an immature infant immune system could mount a genuinely lower initial response that does not itself wane; or (b) the infant response could match the adolescent benchmark and hold flat through the ~12-year window over which currently available immunogenicity studies have followed vaccinated cohorts (8–12), then decline before the exposure window opens. Because the evidence window (≤12 years) ends only a few years before the exposure window begins, no existing study can distinguish between these mechanisms, or between either of them and no shortfall at all. In our simulations we do not choose between mechanisms; instead we treat the effective VE at exposure as the free, swept parameter, varying it across 50%, 70%, and 95% for infant delivery — values chosen to bracket the plausible range implied by both mechanisms without requiring a specific parametric form. This framing lets us report our results as requirements on effective coverage, agnostic to which mechanism, if either, is true.

## Scenario design

We designed a 9-scenario matrix (Table 1) plus a 3 × 3 coverage × efficacy sensitivity grid for infant delivery (see below). All scenarios share Nigeria's historical baseline: an opportunistic screening programme covering ~15% of women aged 30–50 over their lifetime \[ref PMC9116993\], and the 2023–2025 HPV vaccination rollout targeting girls aged 9–14 at aggregate coverages of 27%, 60%, and 60% respectively. Scenarios diverge from 2026 onward. The **base case** is the *status-quo continuation* scenario (S\_sq): adolescent vaccination continues at 60% aggregate coverage post-2026 with the observed education gradient (odds ratio 5 favouring girls who completed primary school), and screening remains at 15% opportunistic coverage. All non-baseline scenarios are compared against this base case and against a *no vaccination* counterfactual (S\_novax).

Two further groups of scenarios address the WHO 90-70-90 elimination targets. In the **screening scale-up group** (S\_sq\_screenup\_or1 and S\_sq\_screenup\_or5), vaccination remains at status quo but screening scales in 2026 to a lifetime-coverage target of 70% aggregate among women aged 30–50, delivered either without an education gradient (edu\_OR = 1: 70% coverage in both primary-completers and non-completers) or with the same gradient we assume for status-quo vaccination (edu\_OR = 5: 90% coverage among primary-completers and 50% among non-completers, aggregating to ~70%). In the **full WHO scale-up group** (S\_who\_or1 and S\_who\_or5), adolescent vaccination additionally scales to 90% coverage in both in-school and out-of-school girls, in parallel with the same two screening variants. Reaching the first "90" of the WHO targets — vaccinating 90% of adolescent girls — requires reaching out-of-school girls at the same rate as those in school, an assumption we return to in the Discussion.

Finally, the **infant delivery group** replaces adolescent vaccination with a single-dose infant programme from 2030 onwards, at 90% coverage uniformly across the birth cohort (breaking the education correlation), with screening at the correlated 90/50 target. Infant-delivery scenarios were run at three effective-VE-at-exposure values — 95% (S\_infant\_full), 70% (S\_infant\_eff70), and 50% (S\_infant\_eff50) — spanning the plausible waning bounds described above. To assess how infant results depend on both coverage and efficacy simultaneously, we additionally ran a 3 × 3 sensitivity grid combining coverage levels of 60%, 75%, and 90% with the three efficacy values (Figure 5). The 60% coverage floor anchors on Nigeria's third-dose DTP coverage (~62% in 2023 \[ref WHO/UNICEF\]), which we take as the empirical lower bound for what an infant HPV programme could realistically achieve without additional platform investment.

We modelled a single-dose quadrivalent vaccine (HPV 16/18/6/11), consistent with the product approved for use in Nigeria and supplied through Gavi. HPV 16 and 18 together are responsible for ~70% of cervical cancers in Nigeria \[ref\]; the vaccine confers 95% efficacy against these types at administration under our base-case assumption, together with cross-protection factors against non-vaccine types as parameterised in HPVsim's default quadrivalent product. A full parameter list, including calibration priors, posterior distributions, and product specifications, is provided in Appendix Table A1.

## Education, vaccine coverage, and screening equity

Nigeria's cervical cancer control challenge is complicated by strong correlations between educational attainment, healthcare access, and both vaccination and screening uptake. To make these correlations explicit and testable in scenario contrasts, we added a lightweight Education module to the microsimulation. Every female agent has a school enrollment state, entering primary school at age 6 with a Bernoulli draw at annual probability 0.85 (Nigeria's approximate net enrollment ratio at ages 9–10), and dropping out each subsequent year through age 14 with annual probability 0.15. Attainment (in years) accumulates over time, and primary completion is defined as reaching 6 years of attainment. Empirically, this reproduces primary completion rates near Nigeria's DHS estimates and yields the approximate 70/30 in-school / out-of-school split at age 9 that we use to calibrate our education-correlated coverage assumptions.

For scenarios with a vaccination education gradient (S\_sq, S\_sq\_screenup\_\*, and the base historical programme), we set the in-school : out-of-school odds ratio to 5 and solve for the coverage probabilities in each stratum that aggregate to the intended total (60% for status quo). For screening, we apply the same edu\_OR = 5 to primary-completers vs. non-completers, either through the correlated 90/50 pair or the equitable 70/70 pair depending on scenario. Infant vaccination is applied uniformly to all birth-cohort members, breaking the vaccination–education correlation by design — this is a key structural argument for infant delivery and is examined explicitly in the Results.

## Screening, treatment, and analysis outputs

Screening uses an HPV DNA test with sensitivity of 90% \[ref hpvsim default\] applied to women aged 30–50 in a per-year Bernoulli draw, whose annual probability we derive from a target lifetime coverage *C* via *p* = 1 − (1 − *C*)^(1/*N*) with *N* = 20 corresponding to the age window, with re-screening gated so that no woman is screened more than once every 10 years. All screen-positives are triaged through a treatment assignment product configured for this study: women with latent, pre-CIN, or CIN infection receive ablation with 80% probability and excision with 20% probability (each at prob = 1.0, meaning every screen-positive receives some form of treatment), while women whose screening detects invasive cancer are all referred to radiation. Treatment efficacies are taken from HPVsim defaults: ablation clears ~93% of lesions and ~80% of viral infection, while excision — the more definitive procedure — clears ~95% of lesions and ~80% of viral infection. This treatment cascade differs from HPVsim's default triage product, which routes only ~5% of pre-CIN screen-positives to any treatment; we override it to reflect a screen-and-treat programme in which linkage to treatment is not the rate-limiting step, and to isolate the effects of coverage and test performance.

## Uncertainty and reporting

To quantify uncertainty, we ran each scenario at every combination of 3 parameter sets and 3 seeds, giving 9 replicates per scenario. Parameter sets were drawn from the top of the calibration posterior (ranked by weighted mismatch score); seeds vary the transmission-model random number stream, capturing stochastic variation in the sexual network and disease progression. Reported outcomes are the mean across replicates; uncertainty ranges shown in figures span the 5th–95th percentile across the 9 replicates. For each simulation, we recorded new cervical cancer cases by year and by birth cohort (using a per-agent tracker for cohorts born pre-2015 and in the six 5-year cohorts spanning 2015–2044), plus HPV prevalence, ASR of cancer incidence, and cases stratified by vaccination × screening status at the time of diagnosis, over the period 2025–2100. Cumulative outcomes are computed to 2100 for the primary results and to 2125 for the pre-2015 cohort tail, which extends beyond 2100 for women alive in 2020.

# Results

## Continuation of Nigeria's current programme leaves most near-term burden untouched

Under a continuation of the current adolescent vaccination programme at 2025 coverage levels (approximately 60% aggregate coverage among girls aged 9–14, with the observed education gradient), and with existing opportunistic screening reaching roughly 15% of women aged 30–50 in their lifetime, we estimate that **1.77 million cervical cancer cases would be averted over 2025–2100** relative to a no-vaccination counterfactual (Figure 2A) — a reduction of 53%. Age-standardised cervical cancer incidence falls from 19.5 per 100,000 in 2025 to **7.2 per 100,000 by 2100** (vs. 25.6 under no vaccination), consistent with the entry of vaccinated cohorts into their peak-risk age band from the mid-2040s onward.

However, the near-term cervical cancer burden in Nigeria is dominated by women who were already beyond the target age for vaccination when the programme launched in 2023. **86% of the cervical cancers projected between 2025 and 2075 occur in women born before 2015** — the birth cohort we hereafter refer to as the *pre-2015 cohort* — with the remainder distributed across the six vaccine-targetable birth cohorts (born 2015–2044). Vaccinating girls aged 9–14 has only a small direct effect on this pre-2015 group (Figure 2B, C): approximately 969,000 cancers over 2025–2100 arise among women born before 2015 even under continued vaccination (down from 1.15 million with no vaccination, a 16% reduction from indirect and cohort-edge effects). Reducing this residual burden depends primarily on the reach of screening and treatment among these women during the remainder of their time in the 30–50 screening window.

## Health outcomes among the six vaccine-targetable birth cohorts

For the six vaccine-targetable birth cohorts (born 2015–2044), continued adolescent vaccination at status-quo coverage would reduce total lifetime cervical cancer cases from approximately 1.36 million (no vaccination) to 403,000 — an aggregate reduction of **70%** across the six cohorts, ranging from 63% in the 2015–2019 cohort (which caught only the tail end of the initial rollout) to 76% in the 2040–2044 cohort (which experiences the full mature programme from age 9). Figure 2C shows the annual cases from each cohort year by year: the six vax-targetable cohorts remain a relatively small share of annual burden through 2075, then dominate as the pre-2015 cohort ages out.

## WHO screening scale-up narrows the pre-2015 gap but with strong education dependence

Scaling opportunistic screening to a WHO-consistent lifetime coverage target of ~70% among women aged 30–50 (delivered as 90% among primary-completers and 50% among non-completers, aggregating to ~70%; scenario S_sq_screenup_or5) averts an additional **442,000 cancers** over 2025–2100 (28% of the S_sq residual), of which **278,000 are in the pre-2015 cohort** — the women vaccination cannot reach (Figure 3B). Even so, ~715,000 pre-2015 cancers remain even under the fully scaled screening programme; the residual reflects the fraction of women who age out of the 30–50 screening window before 2026, plus women reached only late in that window, plus test/treatment cascade losses.

The story here depends strongly on whether screening scale-up is correlated with the same educational determinants as vaccination. Under our baseline assumption that women who did not complete primary school are 5-fold less likely to reach lifetime screening (edu_OR = 5), we estimate **6% more cervical cancers in the vaccine-targetable cohorts** (~16,000 additional cases) than would be predicted under the counterfactual assumption of equitably delivered screening at the same 70% aggregate coverage (S_sq_screenup_or1). This is a meaningful bias if planning assumes education-neutral delivery when in fact the same women miss both interventions.

## Infant vaccination trades the education correlation for durability risk

Fully scaling both vaccination and screening to WHO 90-70-90 targets (S_who_or5) would avert ~600,000 cancers over 2025–2100 relative to status quo — including a 56% reduction in cancers among the vax-targetable birth cohorts (Figure 4). However, reaching this scenario requires vaccinating 90% of adolescent girls, which in turn requires reaching out-of-school girls at the same coverage as those in school — an assumption that is not currently met and that, if unrealised, would leave overall adolescent coverage at approximately 60% (i.e. a continuation of S_sq).

Infant delivery offers an alternative route to high coverage that structurally removes the vaccination-education correlation, since delivery through the routine childhood series does not depend on school attendance. Under our baseline assumption that infant vaccine efficacy is equivalent to adolescent efficacy (95% at exposure), a programme reaching 90% of infants (S_infant_full) achieves outcomes broadly comparable to full WHO scale-up — 197,600 cancers in the vax-targetable cohorts vs. 178,700 under S_who_or5 (51% vs. 56% reduction from status quo). The remaining gap reflects the fact that S_who catches older adolescent cohorts (born 2009–2016) that fall between the historical adolescent programme and the 2030 infant switch-over.

The strength of the infant strategy erodes if either coverage falls below 90% or efficacy falls below the adolescent benchmark (Figure 5). At the empirically-grounded DTP3-anchored coverage of 60% and hypothetical 50% effective VE at exposure (representing rapid waning between infant vaccination and peak HPV exposure), infant delivery averts only 20% of vax-targetable-cohort cancers — barely better than status quo. Even at 90% coverage, an effective VE at exposure of 50% averts only 40% of these cancers. Combining Equation 1 with the observed adolescent programme efficacy (~95%) suggests that an infant programme would need effective VE at exposure ≥ 63% at 90% coverage, or ≥ 90% at 60% coverage, to be non-inferior to Nigeria's current 85% adolescent reach. Nevertheless, at coverage levels around 60% where the two strategies deliver comparable overall reductions, the infant strategy's strength rests on breaking the education correlation: at those coverage levels the infant strategy still averts more cancers in the historically hardest-to-reach subgroups by structurally removing the vaccination-education overlap.

# Discussion

Using a Nigeria-calibrated HPV transmission model, we quantified three interlocking constraints on cervical cancer control over the next 75 years: (i) most of the near-term cancer burden falls on women born before the country's 2023 adolescent vaccination programme could reach them, and can only be addressed through screening; (ii) opportunistic and even scaled screening in Nigeria is likely to be strongly mediated by education, meaning that the same women who missed vaccination are also less likely to reach screening, compounding the inequity; and (iii) infant vaccination offers a structural route around this cascade correlation, but only if it can achieve coverage and durability that meet or exceed the requirements set out in Equation 1. These findings extend previous modelling work on infant HPV delivery (\[refs\]) by embedding the analysis in a real programmatic setting and by making the vaccination-education correlation explicit.

## Programmatic feasibility of infant HPV delivery

Nigeria's third-dose DTP coverage was approximately 62% in 2023 (\[ref WHO/UNICEF\]), which we take as the empirical floor for what an infant HPV programme could realistically achieve using the existing platform without additional investment. Under this coverage assumption, our results show that infant delivery would avert only 20–37% of vaccine-targetable cohort cancers depending on effective VE at exposure (Figure 5), which is comparable to or worse than the 55–58% averted under continued adolescent delivery at Nigeria's current 60% aggregate coverage combined with WHO screening scale-up. Reaching the 90% coverage assumed in most of our analyses would require the same programmatic investment as reaching the WHO 90% adolescent target — leaving the choice between the two delivery strategies driven not by *whether* high coverage can be reached, but by which coverage is easier to sustain equitably. Delivery through the routine childhood immunisation series has documented programmatic advantages: coverage in Nigeria and other sub-Saharan settings is more even across urban/rural and educational strata than school-based delivery, and per-dose delivery costs are lower when added to existing infant contact points (\[refs\]). Against these advantages must be set the cost of vaccinating two cohorts in parallel during any transition period, the possible need for multi-dose schedules if single-dose immunogenicity is insufficient at infant ages, and the opportunity cost of not investing in an adolescent-facing health platform that could deliver other adolescent services alongside HPV vaccination.

## Biological uncertainty: durability, immune maturity, and the single-dose assumption

The core biological uncertainty for infant HPV delivery is whether protection persists across the ~15–25-year interval between infant vaccination and peak HPV exposure (Nigeria's median age at first sex is 17.9 years (19)). The five studies most often cited for HPV vaccine durability (8–12) are more heterogeneous than a single citation cluster suggests, and none directly supports extrapolation across this interval. Three (8–10) follow the same Costa Rica Vaccine Trial cohort, vaccinated at ages 18–25 and followed for a median of ~11 years: one (8) reports HPV16/18 infection durability, a second (9) reports cross-protection against non-vaccine types (HPV31/33/45) rather than vaccine-type durability, and the third (10) reports the strongest endpoint of the five — HPV16/18-associated CIN2+/CIN3 (precancer) — for the trial's three-dose recipients. The India trial (11) enrolled the youngest and most policy-relevant cohort (girls aged 10–18, closer to the 9–14 target of Nigeria's adolescent programme, and including single-dose recipients) but followed them for 9 years against a persistent-infection endpoint. The Kenyan single-dose trial (12) enrolled young women aged 15–20 and reported its primary persistent-infection endpoint at month 18. In short, no cited study measures durability against invasive cancer, none extends past ~11 years, and none enrolled anyone younger than 10 — let alone infants. The closest available age match is an immunogenicity (not efficacy) study in Tanzanian girls aged 9–14 — the same age range as Nigeria's adolescent programme — showing single-dose antibody titres stable from month 12 to month 60 (20); even so, 5 years falls well short of the 15–25-year horizon required for infant delivery, and antibody titres are not a validated correlate of clinical protection for HPV vaccines. Because our required durability horizon begins only a few years after the longest available follow-up ends, current evidence cannot distinguish a genuinely durable response from one that has simply not yet had time to wane.

Rather than model a specific waning function, we treated the effective vaccine efficacy at exposure as the varied parameter (Figure 1B, C), which is agnostic to why efficacy at exposure might fall short of the adolescent benchmark. We illustrate two distinct, non-exclusive mechanisms consistent with the evidence gap above: (a) an immature infant immune system could mount a genuinely lower initial response that does not itself wane; or (b) the infant response could match the adolescent benchmark and hold flat through the observed evidence window before declining ahead of the exposure window. Both are equally compatible with a literature that has never followed anyone long enough, or young enough, to distinguish them. What matters for cancer averted is the residual protection when HPV is encountered, regardless of mechanism; our results should therefore be interpreted as requirements on effective efficacy at exposure — not as forecasts contingent on a particular immunological model.

A related and less discussed uncertainty is whether the efficacy evidence above — drawn entirely from participants aged 10 and older — applies at all to infants vaccinated in the first months of life. Infant and adolescent immune systems differ systematically (e.g. maternal antibody interference and the balance of innate versus adaptive responses in early life, which is why several routine infant vaccines are deliberately timed after the first year of life), and the direction of the net effect on HPV vaccine response is not established: there is no empirical basis to assume that infant efficacy at exposure will match adolescent efficacy, and equally no basis to assume it will not. This uncertainty maps onto mechanism (a) above, just as the durability question maps onto mechanism (b); our efficacy sensitivity (50–95% at exposure) accommodates both without adjudicating between them. Similarly, the sufficiency of a single dose has been demonstrated in adolescent and young-adult recipients (11,12,17) but has not been tested in infants; a multi-dose schedule would raise per-fully-immunised-child costs and could reduce attainable coverage. These are precisely the empirical questions that our analysis is intended to motivate — not to resolve.

## Long-horizon comparability and demographic change

Our projections extend to 2100, a horizon over which Nigeria's population is projected to more than double (\[ref UN WPP\]). The counterfactual and intervention scenarios share the same demographic inputs, so the *relative* effects we report (cancers averted, percentage reductions in cohort burden) are robust to demographic uncertainty; the absolute counts scale with the projected population and should be interpreted as such. We treated cervical cancer incidence, not deaths, as the primary outcome; treatment access for cancer diagnosed at younger ages varies substantially in Nigeria and would compound demographic assumptions further.

## Limitations

Our findings depend on several simplifying assumptions. First, the vaccination-education correlation is parameterised via a single odds ratio (edu_OR = 5), which is a summary of empirical patterns rather than a directly-fitted quantity; a smaller correlation would reduce the equity contrast between adolescent and infant delivery. Second, we assumed a fixed screening test with a fixed sensitivity throughout — evolving diagnostic performance (e.g. self-sampling for HPV DNA) would shift screening effectiveness. Third, we modelled a single-dose quadrivalent vaccine on the assumption that this remains the product supplied through Gavi; a switch to the 9-valent product would increase cross-protection and modestly widen the gap between vaccinated and unvaccinated cohorts. Fourth, we did not have Nigeria-specific data on HPV genotype distribution in low-grade precancerous lesions, so our persistence estimates rely on genotype distribution in high-grade lesions. Fifth, our sexual behaviour inputs draw on publicly-available survey data (18) that is subject to reporting bias.

## Conclusions

Nigeria's cervical cancer trajectory over the next 75 years is a story of two problems that cannot be solved by the same intervention. The women who will bear the near-term burden aged out of the vaccination window before the programme launched, and the near-term response has to be scaling screening among them — imperfectly, because education-mediated inequity in screening access means that the same women who missed vaccination will also be hardest to reach through screening. For the vaccine-targetable birth cohorts, the equity argument for infant delivery is compelling in principle: routine childhood immunisation decouples HPV protection from school attendance and from the cascade of educational determinants that mediates access to other services. Whether that principle translates into practice hinges on empirical questions that only prospective studies can resolve: how durable is single-dose infant immunity across two-plus decades, what fraction of infant HPV coverage can Nigeria sustain through the routine platform, and how do the delivery costs compare over a phased transition. In the interim, sustaining and equitably scaling the adolescent vaccination programme — with focused attention on out-of-school girls — together with a real investment in population-based screening for the pre-vaccine cohort remains the most consequential lever available.
